content.title: About
content.content: Beet greens are the edible leafy tops of the beet plant, harvested early in the growing season. The leaves are tender, slightly bitter, and deep green. They are eaten raw, added to salads, smoothies, or lightly cooked as a vegetable.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beet greens are rich in chlorophyll, giving them a vivid green color.
In many Eastern European cuisines they are a traditional spring salad ingredient.
The greens can also be used as animal feed, but are prized for human consumption because of their nutrient density.
They are sometimes confused with mustard greens, though they have a milder flavor.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K supports blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: These nutrients aid vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C provides antioxidant protection and helps iron absorption.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Beet greens supply calcium, magnesium, and iron, important for bones and blood.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to beet greens.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Beet greens contain oxalates, which in large amounts can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Choose organic or thoroughly wash the greens to reduce exposure to chemicals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the leaves raw in salads, blend them into smoothies, roll them in wraps, or quickly sauté with garlic. Rinse well and pat dry before consumption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store beet greens in the refrigerator in a sealed container or a bag with a small amount of moisture for up to 3–5 days. For longer storage, blanch and freeze the greens.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with a tomato-based sauce and added vegetables is a home recipe that combines whole‑grain noodles, a flavorful tomato sauce, and a mix of vegetables such as carrots, zucchini, and bell pepper. The dish is rich in fiber, vitamins, and minerals, providing a steady release of energy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta contains more fiber and protein than traditional white‑flour pasta.
Tomatoes are an excellent source of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
Adding a variety of vegetables boosts the content of vitamins A, C, and B‑complex, as well as minerals like potassium and magnesium.
A homemade sauce lets you control salt and sugar levels, making the meal healthier.
Cooking tomatoes and vegetables over moderate heat preserves most of their nutrients.

items.title: High in Fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta and vegetables support healthy digestion and promote satiety.

items.title: Source of Complex Carbohydrates
items.content: The pasta provides a stable blood‑glucose level, offering sustained energy throughout the day.

items.title: Lycopene and Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes supply lycopene, which may reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and certain cancers.

items.title: Vitamins and Minerals
items.content: Vegetables add vitamins A, C, K and potassium, supporting heart and muscle function.

items.title: Low in Saturated Fat
items.content: The dish is prepared without butter or heavy cream, making it suitable for low‑saturated‑fat diets.

items.title: Gluten Sensitivity
items.content: Whole grain pasta contains gluten, so individuals with celiac disease or gluten intolerance should use a gluten‑free alternative.

items.title: Sodium Content
items.content: If the sauce is prepared with a lot of added salt, it may increase the risk of high blood pressure.

items.title: Tomato Acidity
items.content: People with gastritis or acid reflux may experience increased heartburn from tomato‑based sauces.

content.title: How to Prepare and Serve
content.content: Cook the whole grain pasta until al dente, drain, reserving a cup of pasta water. Sauté finely chopped vegetables in a pan, add the tomato sauce, and simmer for 10‑15 minutes, thinning with reserved water if needed. Toss the pasta with the sauce, optionally garnish with fresh herbs or grated Parmesan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Keep dry pasta separate in a cool, dry place; reheat with a splash of water on the stovetop or in the microwave.

pizza-with-meat-other-than-pepperoni-fro.title: Pizza with meat (no pepperoni), school lunch, medium crust

content.title: About
content.content: A pizza topped with a mix of meats such as ham, chicken, or beef, without pepperoni, served as part of a school lunch. The medium crust (3415) provides a balanced crunch and softness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional school pizza is often produced in large batches to ensure consistent taste and quality.
Meat toppings without pepperoni usually contain less sodium than classic pepperoni.
The medium crust (size 3415) was designed for an optimal dough‑to‑topping ratio, making the pizza easy to hold.
School menus often fortify pizza with vitamins and minerals to meet children’s nutritional requirements.
The dough for a medium crust typically uses a modest amount of yeast, allowing faster baking in industrial ovens.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Meat toppings provide high‑quality protein essential for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat supplies heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Meat and whole‑grain dough contribute B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Moderate fiber
items.content: If whole‑grain flour is used, the crust adds dietary fiber beneficial for digestion.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The cheese layer provides calcium important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cured meat slices and cheese can increase overall salt intake, which should be monitored.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Meat toppings and cheese add saturated fats, which may be a concern for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to milk proteins.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional crust contains gluten, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pizza is conveniently eaten by hand, cut into bite‑size slices. Adding fresh vegetables such as tomatoes or cucumber, or a sprinkle of herbs, can boost its nutritional profile.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in an oven or microwave to keep the crust crisp.

content.title: About
content.content: Butter‑flavored microwave popcorn is a ready‑to‑cook bag containing corn kernels, butter seasoning, and oil. When heated in a microwave, the kernels pop into a light, crunchy, and aromatic snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is one of the oldest snacks, enjoyed by ancient American civilizations.
Microwave popcorn was introduced in the 1980s and quickly became popular for its convenience.
The butter flavor is usually created with a blend of natural and artificial flavorings plus a small amount of oil.
One bag typically yields 2‑3 servings, perfect for movie nights.
Popcorn is gluten‑free, making it suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Low in calories when eaten plain
items.content: Popcorn contains little fat and calories as long as extra butter, oil, or sugar are not added.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Corn kernels are rich in fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Popcorn provides polyphenols that may help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for those avoiding gluten.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Quickly prepared and gentle on the stomach, making it a convenient snack.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Some varieties contain a lot of salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Additives and flavorings
items.content: Artificial flavorings may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Risk of steam burns
items.content: Steam released from the bag after microwaving can cause burns, so open the bag carefully.

items.title: Calorie increase with toppings
items.content: Adding butter, cheese sauce, or caramel dramatically raises the calorie count.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place the bag in the microwave and follow the instructions on the package (usually 2‑3 minutes on high). Let it sit for a minute after cooking, then open the bag, stir to distribute the butter flavor evenly, and enjoy.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened bag in a cool, dry place away from moisture. After opening, keep the popcorn in an airtight container to maintain crunchiness and prevent moisture absorption.

content.title: About
content.content: The white hot‑dog roll is a soft, slightly sweet wheat‑flour bun designed for serving sausages, frankfurters and a variety of toppings. It has a small cylindrical shape, about 12 cm long, making it easy to hold in the hand.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: These buns are a staple of street food in the United States and Canada.
The dough usually contains a modest amount of sugar and butter, giving it a more tender crumb than regular bread.
Some recipes add milk or egg yolk to achieve a golden crust.
Buns are often served warm, which keeps them soft and aromatic.
In Russia a similar product is sold as “sausage buns,” often frozen for convenience.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Provides a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains modest protein
items.content: Wheat flour contributes a small amount of plant‑based protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Enriched flour can supply B1, B2 and niacin, which support metabolism.

items.title: Versatile pairing
items.content: Neutral flavor allows the bun to complement a wide range of fillings, vegetables, proteins and sauces.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of carbs and a little fat makes the bun satisfying, helping to curb hunger.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Contains wheat flour, so it is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Can cause a rapid rise in blood sugar, which may be problematic for diabetics.

items.title: Salt and sugar content
items.content: Some commercial recipes add salt and sugar, which should be considered in restricted diets.

items.title: Preservatives in industrial versions
items.content: Frozen or pre‑packaged buns may contain additives that not everyone tolerates well.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Warm the bun in an oven or microwave for 30–60 seconds, split it lengthwise and place a sausage, frankfurter, vegetables, cheese, sauces or any favorite toppings. Common additions include mustard, ketchup, mayo and fresh veggies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen buns in a freezer at –18 °C. After thawing, store in an airtight container for up to 2 days. Fresh buns stored in the refrigerator stay good for 5–7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Pho is a traditional Vietnamese soup made from a fragrant broth, rice noodles, fresh herbs, and thinly sliced meat (usually beef). The broth is simmered with bones, spices (star anise, cinnamon, clove) and ginger, giving the dish a deep, aromatic flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pho originated in northern Vietnam in the early 20th century and quickly became the national dish.
It is traditionally served with lime, soy sauce, chili and fresh herbs such as basil, mint and cilantro.
There are several regional variants, most notably pho bo (beef) and pho ga (chicken).
Rice noodles are cooked “al dente” to retain a pleasant chew in the hot broth.
Vietnamese people enjoy pho for breakfast, lunch or dinner.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The broth is made from bones without excessive added fat, making the dish light.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and herbs supply B1, B2, B6 and B12 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Bones release calcium, magnesium and phosphorus into the broth, beneficial for bones and nerves.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory herbs
items.content: Ginger, cinnamon and clove have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Broth is often salty; people with hypertension should monitor salt intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: While rice noodles are gluten‑free, some sauces (e.g., regular soy sauce) may contain gluten.

items.title: Calorie‑dense toppings
items.content: Fried onions, bean sprouts or large amounts of meat can increase the calorie count of a serving.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve pho piping hot, adding noodles, meat and fresh herbs to the broth. Finish with lime juice, soy sauce, chili and bean sprouts to taste. Gently stir the noodles so they absorb the broth’s flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the broth in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Store dry noodles separately; reheat the soup to a boil before serving. Freeze broth in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months.
